meetings.title: Q4 Product Alignment: Insights 2.0
segments: Okay, I think the recording's on.
Hi everyone. Let's give people one more minute, I know a couple of folks are coming straight from other calls.
Morning. Or, I guess, evening for Elena.
It's almost eight here, yes.
But I have a very large coffee, so I'm fully present.
Brave.
Can everyone hear me okay?
I switched to the headset.
My laptop mic was doing the robot voice thing in the design crit yesterday.
You sound great, Marcus. Much better than yesterday, honestly.
Ha. Thanks. I'll take it.
Hey all, sorry. I was sitting in the old Zoom link by myself for two minutes wondering where everyone was.
That's on me, I moved the invite and the old link stayed in the description. Sorry, Daniel.
No worries. I got some email done.
I'm here too, I just had my camera off, I'm eating lunch. Hi.
Hi Priya. Okay, we're just missing Aisha.
She was on with the Globex security team this morning, so I'm guessing that ran long.
Hi, sorry, sorry. I'm here.
The Globex conversation is actually really relevant to today, so, good timing I guess.
Perfect segue. Okay, let me frame this, and then we'll go around.
The goal for this hour is to leave with three things.
A locked scope for Insights 2.0.
A beta date we actually believe in.
And a clear call on SAML SSO versus the Jira integration, because I don't think we can staff both this quarter, and I'd rather we decide that together than have it decided by default.
Rough agenda. Tom and Aisha on customer signal, maybe ten minutes.
Priya on where the clustering model actually is.
Marcus has the new dashboard.
Then Daniel on integrations and SSO, Elena on launch, and I want to save the last five minutes for owners and dates.
Does that sound okay? Anything missing?
Can we make sure we talk about capacity before we commit to any dates?
I don't want us to walk out of here with a date that assumes the platform team is at a hundred percent, because we're not.
Yes. Totally fair. Let's do that right after Priya, before the design walkthrough.
Great, thanks.
Actually, Raj, before Tom starts.
Can you give everyone thirty seconds on the ingest outage?
I know a few people here haven't read the postmortem yet, and it's relevant to the capacity conversation.
Sure. So, two weeks ago, ingest was delayed for about six hours.
Feedback kept arriving, we didn't lose anything, but it wasn't showing up in workspaces.
Two hundred and twelve workspaces were affected, mostly the larger ones.
Root cause was a schema migration that took a lock on the events table during peak traffic.
The queue backed up behind it, and our alerting only looked at error rates, not at how far behind the queue was.
So we found out from a customer, which is the part I'm least happy about.
Yeah, we got fourteen tickets and two escalations that morning.
Brightline was one of them, actually.
Of course it was.
The queue lag alert shipped last week, so that part's fixed.
What's left is moving to online migrations, so a schema change can never lock a hot table again.
That's the hardening work I mentioned.
It's about one engineer until the end of the month.
Does that affect the clustering jobs?
We read from the same events table.
It does, in a good way.
Once the migrations are online, your nightly re-cluster can run without us worrying about locks at all.
Okay. Thanks Raj. And thanks for being so direct in the postmortem, it was really clear.
Thanks. Okay, over to Tom.
Tom, do you want to kick us off?
Sure. So I pulled the last ninety days of churn and downgrade conversations.
It's forty-one accounts total. The top reason, by a wide margin, is still some version of 'we have the data but nobody reads it.'
Customers export the feedback, it sits in a spreadsheet, and whatever insight is in there never makes it into an actual product decision.
That was the stated reason in seventeen of the forty-one.
Seventeen of forty-one. Wow.
Yeah. And that's just the ones who said it out loud.
The second cluster is integration gaps.
People want the feedback to show up where they already work, so Slack and Jira come up constantly.
Eleven accounts mentioned Jira by name.
Eleven, okay. That's higher than what I had in my doc.
It's eleven if you count the ones where it came up on a renewal call, not just in a ticket.
I can send you the list.
Yes please, that'd be great.
And then the third reason, which is newer, is accuracy of the auto-tagging.
A few customers, Brightline was the loudest, have said the tags feel random and they've just stopped trusting them.
Olivia over there told me they turned tagging off entirely for their support team.
Do you know if that's the old keyword tagger or the model we piloted in August?
It's the old one. Brightline wasn't in the pilot.
Okay, good. That actually matters a lot, I'll come back to it.
I want to give one more concrete example, because the numbers can feel abstract.
Harbor and Pine, the outdoor retailer, downgraded from Business to Pro last month.
Their CX lead told me she spends every Monday morning copying support tickets into a slide deck for their exec meeting.
By hand. She said, 'I'm paying you to do exactly this, and I'm still doing it myself.'
Oof.
That's painful.
That's basically the Themes pitch in one sentence.
It really is. And the other pattern is Slack.
Separate from Jira, a lot of people just want a weekly summary pushed into a Slack channel, so the product team sees it without logging in.
That came up in, I think, nine of the forty-one conversations.
Daniel, we have a Slack app already, right?
We do, but it only sends alerts.
Like, 'a new comment matched your saved filter.'
It doesn't do summaries. Honestly, most people turn it off after a week because it's too noisy.
Okay, let's keep that in mind for when Marcus shows the design.
The good news is the pilot accounts.
Eight accounts used the theme clustering prototype.
Six of them asked, completely unprompted, when they can have it for real.
Sana at Lakeshore Bank said, and I wrote this down, 'this is the first time the tool told me something I didn't already know.'
Oh, can I steal that quote for the launch?
I'll ask her. I think she'd say yes, she's been a big fan.
That's a great line.
It really is. Okay. Aisha, sales side?
Yeah. So I'll be blunt.
We have two enterprise deals, Globex and Arcadia Health, that are blocked on SAML SSO.
Not slowed down, blocked. Their security teams will not sign without it.
Together that's about four hundred and twenty thousand in annual contract value.
Sorry, four twenty?
Four twenty. Globex is about two sixty and Arcadia is about one sixty.
And on the Globex call this morning, Victor, their CISO, was really clear.
It's SAML plus audit logs, and he wants a date in writing before they'll move to procurement.
Is there a reason Victor needs the date in writing now?
Is something forcing their timeline?
Yes, their fiscal year ends in about eight weeks, and the budget for this is use it or lose it.
If procurement doesn't start in the next few weeks, the deal slides into next year and gets re-approved from scratch.
Which, at Globex, means another four months.
Okay, that's a real forcing function.
It is. And to be clear, they don't need SSO live to sign.
They need a committed date and the questionnaire answers.
They'll accept a contract that says SSO within a set number of weeks of signature.
That's really helpful. So the date is what unblocks them, not the feature itself.
Did he say which identity provider they're on?
Okta. And Arcadia is on Azure AD.
Their IT lead, Imran, brought it up in the first ten minutes of discovery.
Okay. So we'd need both from day one. That's useful to know.
And for context on Arcadia, it's a big deployment.
About three thousand support agents across their patient services teams.
They want to pull in feedback from their patient portal, their call center notes, and app store reviews.
Patient portal feedback, okay. That's going to be very sensitive text.
Yes. Their security review will go deep on that, I'm sure.
The other one I want to mention is Kestrel Logistics.
Mid-market, about four hundred employees, I did discovery with them last week.
They're not blocked on anything, they just really, really want the themes view.
Grace, their VP of operations, would be a perfect design partner.
Oh, nice. Put her on my list.
And one competitive data point.
The competitor that beat us twice is charging fifteen dollars per seat per month for their AI add-on.
Customers are grumbling about that model, so there might be an opening for us on pricing.
Interesting. Let's hold that for the pricing discussion at the end.
And to be fair to the Jira side, Jira comes up in almost every mid-market demo.
But nobody has actually walked away from a deal over it.
With SSO, people walk away.
That's the difference for me.
That's a really useful distinction.
For what it's worth, that matches what I see on retention.
For most accounts Jira is a nice-to-have.
Tom, of those eleven Jira accounts, how many actually churned, versus just asked for it?
I think two churned. The rest either downgraded or just complained.
But I'd want to double check that before anyone quotes it.
Okay. Can you confirm that number after the call?
It matters for the SSO decision.
Yep. I'll confirm the Jira churn number and send it to you and Daniel today.
Thanks. Anything else on signal before we go to Priya?
One quick thing, on competitive.
Two of the deals we lost last month went to a competitor who's pitching 'AI insights.'
I honestly don't think their product is better than ours.
But their story is simpler.
We keep saying 'feedback analytics,' and I think buyers hear 'another dashboard.'
Elena, what does their demo actually look like? Have you seen it?
I watched the recording from their last webinar.
It opens on a single screen that says 'here are the five things your customers are upset about this week,' with a big number next to each one.
That's it. No filters, no dashboards, no setup.
It's very simple, and honestly, it lands.
That's almost exactly our Themes home screen.
Just with less in it.
Right. Which is why I think we can win this.
The difference is what happens when you click in.
From what customers tell us, their themes are hard to correct, and there's no way to trace a theme back to the actual comments. We have both.
Traceability is a big deal for enterprise buyers.
They always ask 'where did this come from.'
Good. Hold that thought, it's going to matter for the launch story.
A hundred percent. I hear that in demos.
Noted. Let's come back to that when we get to launch, because I think it connects to Marcus's work too.
Okay. Priya, where are we with the model?
Okay, let me share my screen.
One sec. Can you all see the eval sheet?
Yep, we can see it.
Great. So, quick recap for anyone who hasn't been following closely.
The clustering model takes raw feedback, so support tickets, NPS comments, call notes, app reviews, and groups them into themes.
Then it writes a short label and a one-paragraph summary for each theme.
The August pilot version had a precision of seventy-one percent on our labeled set.
Meaning, when it put a comment into a theme, the comment actually belonged there about seven times out of ten.
And the target we set for GA was eighty-five, right?
Eighty-five, yes. With the new embedding model and a re-ranking step I added last sprint, we're at seventy-nine percent on the same set.
So real progress, but we're not there yet.
Sorry, can I ask a dumb question?
What does seventy-nine actually feel like for a customer? Is that noticeable?
Not a dumb question at all.
At seventy-nine, if you open a theme with twenty comments in it, maybe four of them look out of place.
People notice that. At eighty-five it's about three, and in the pilot interviews that's roughly where people stopped commenting on it.
That tracks with Brightline. With the old tagger they were seeing something like one in three tagged wrong.
Right, the old keyword tagger is closer to sixty percent.
So even seventy-nine is a big jump from what most customers have today.
What gets us from seventy-nine to eighty-five?
Two things. First, a bigger and better labeled set.
Our eval set is only eight hundred comments, and it's skewed toward SaaS companies.
I want two thousand, with retail and healthcare properly represented, because that's where it's weakest.
Second, letting users merge and split themes, and learning from that.
Honestly, the merge and split feedback is the biggest lever we have.
But it needs design, and it needs the beta to actually generate the data.
Do you have a feel for how long the merge and split data would take to move the number?
Rough guess. If twenty design partners each do something like thirty merges or splits a week, that's six hundred corrections a week.
In the pilot, a few hundred corrections moved precision by two or three points.
So, four to six weeks of beta usage to get from seventy-nine to eighty-five, if the partners are active.
They'll be active. I'll make that part of the design partner deal.
That would really help. Inactive partners are the risk, not the model.
The merge and split interaction is in the new prototype, by the way.
I'll show it in a bit.
Oh, nice. I didn't know it had made it in.
Can I show a couple of the failure cases?
I think it helps to see what seventy-nine percent actually looks like, rather than just the number.
Please.
Okay, so this is the most common failure.
The model merged a theme about 'invoices are confusing' with a theme about 'billing failed.'
To the model they look the same, it's all billing words.
But to a product team those are completely different problems, one is a design issue and one is an outage.
Yeah, those should never be together.
Right. The second failure is themes that are too broad.
Like, 'the app is slow.'
It's technically correct, but it has four hundred comments in it, and nobody can act on it.
Inside that theme there are really three things: slow search, slow exports, and the mobile app on older phones.
That's exactly what the split interaction is for.
Exactly. And the third thing, which I care about a lot, is the theme summaries.
The model writes a short paragraph for each theme.
I built a check that verifies each sentence in the summary is actually supported by the comments in the theme.
Right now about four percent of summary sentences make a claim that isn't supported.
Four percent of sentences, or four percent of summaries?
Sentences. So on a typical theme page you might see one shaky sentence every few themes.
We drop anything the check flags before it's shown, so users don't see them.
But it's why I don't want to rush GA.
On the labels themselves. Some of the pilot labels read a bit robotic.
Like 'Negative sentiment regarding onboarding process.'
Could they sound more like how a person would write them?
Agreed. We've been saying labels should be short noun phrases, like 'Confusing invoice layout,' not sentences.
Priya and I talked about putting examples right into the prompt.
Yes, that's easy to change.
I'll add label style examples to the prompt this sprint.
And Tom, for your team's labeling days, I'll write up labeling guidelines with examples before they start, so everyone labels the same way.
That would help a lot, thank you.
Priya, one thing I want to flag, for healthcare specifically.
If we're sending Arcadia's feedback to a model, their security team is going to ask what happens to patient information in those comments.
People put all kinds of things in support tickets.
Yes. We already redact emails and phone numbers before anything goes to the model.
We don't do names or anything like medical record numbers yet.
I'd want to add a proper PII redaction pass before any healthcare customer is in the beta.
That will absolutely come up with Arcadia.
Their security review is forty pages.
Okay. Priya, can you and Daniel scope the redaction pass, so we know what it takes before we invite any healthcare accounts?
Yes. Daniel and I will scope the PII redaction pass this week.
Works for me.
Can I ask about latency?
Last time I looked, clustering a big workspace was taking, what, forty seconds?
For the largest pilot account, about thirty-eight seconds at p95.
For most workspaces it's under ten.
The big cost is re-clustering everything every time new feedback comes in.
What I'd propose is incremental assignment, where new comments get placed into existing themes right away, and then we only do a full re-cluster nightly.
That's how I'd want to do it.
I really don't want a user staring at a spinner for forty seconds.
Can we set a budget?
Something like p95 under three seconds for anything the user is actually waiting on.
For incremental assignment, three seconds is doable.
For the full re-cluster, no, that has to be a background job.
Background job is fine. We have the job queue from the exports work, we can reuse that.
Okay, so the proposal is: incremental assignment in the product, a nightly full re-cluster in the background, and a p95 of three seconds for anything the user waits on. Does anyone object?
From a design side, can we show when the themes were last fully refreshed?
Something like 'themes updated overnight, new comments are added as they arrive.'
People get suspicious if numbers move and they don't know why.
Yes, and we can show a small badge on themes that grew a lot since the last full refresh.
Nice. Let's include that in the prototype.
No, makes sense.
Makes sense to me. It also means I can design for themes updating quietly instead of a big loading state.
Great. Priya, can you own getting the labeled set to two thousand?
Yes. I'll need about three days of labeling help though.
I was going to ask Tom's team, because they know how customers actually talk about problems.
We can do that. I can give you two people for the back half of this week.
Perfect. Then I'll run the eval on the two thousand comment set and share the precision report by the middle of next week.
Thank you.
Okay. Raj, you wanted to talk capacity. Go for it.
Yeah. So, just to be honest with everyone.
The platform team is five engineers.
One of them is on call every week, so realistically it's four.
Right now we still have the ingest pipeline hardening from the outage two weeks ago, and that's not optional.
That's probably one engineer until the end of the month.
So I have three people for new work.
Three people.
Three. And here's roughly how I see it.
Incremental assignment plus the background re-cluster is maybe one and a half people for three weeks.
SAML SSO done properly, meaning Okta and Azure AD, audit logs, SCIM later, is two people for four to five weeks.
And the Jira integration is two people for about four weeks, because their API is, uh, a lot.
How confident are you in those numbers, Raj?
Like, plus or minus what?
The Insights work, pretty confident, maybe plus or minus a week.
SAML, less so. The protocol part is well understood, but every identity provider has quirks, and Azure AD in particular has surprised people.
We also need real test tenants, not just mocks.
I can get us an Okta developer tenant today, and I'll ask Arcadia if they'd give us a sandbox Azure AD app.
They offered to help with testing.
That would take a lot of risk out of it.
Real tenants are the difference between five weeks and eight.
It really is a lot.
It's a lot.
So I can do Insights 2.0 plus one of SSO or Jira.
Not both. Not this quarter, not with three people, unless we want to cut corners on the outage work, and I really don't.
What if we did a much lighter Jira thing?
Like, just a 'create issue' button, one way, no sync at all?
That's a lot smaller. Maybe a week and a half.
But I'd still be taking that week and a half from somewhere.
Could we borrow anyone from the growth team for a few weeks?
I asked. They're mid-way through the billing migration, and I don't think pulling someone off billing is a good idea.
That's the kind of thing that goes badly if you rush it.
Fair. No, let's not touch billing.
Okay, let's hold the SSO and Jira question for a few minutes, because I want Daniel to walk through it properly with the full picture.
Marcus, let's see the dashboard first.
Okay, sharing now. Let me know when you can see the Figma file.
Yep, it's up.
Cool. So this is the new home screen for Insights 2.0.
The big change is that the default view is Themes, not the Feed.
Today, you land on a list of raw feedback, newest first.
Which is exactly the 'nobody reads it' problem Tom just described.
Here, you land on the top themes this week, ranked by volume and by how fast they're growing.
Oh, I like the little growth arrow.
Thanks. So each theme card has the AI label, the number of comments, the trend over the last four weeks, and three representative quotes.
We tested showing five quotes, and people just stopped reading after the second one, so we went down to three.
Sorry, I think I dropped for a few seconds there.
My internet is doing its evening thing.
Did I miss anything on the cards?
Just that each card shows three representative quotes.
We tested five and people stopped reading after two.
Got it, thanks. I'm back.
What's the source mix? Can I tell whether a theme is mostly support tickets or mostly NPS?
Yes, there's a small breakdown bar under the count.
Hover it and you get the exact split by source.
Great, that's important for sales-led accounts.
Then if you click into a theme, you get the full list of comments, and this is where merge and split live.
You can drag one theme onto another to merge them, or you select a handful of comments and split them out into a new theme.
And every merge or split gets logged as a training signal?
That's the idea. We'd show a small toast like 'thanks, this improves your themes,' so people know it's actually doing something, and it's not just busywork.
Love that. That's exactly the data I need.
Two more things on this screen, and they connect to what Tom said about Slack.
First, every theme has a 'share' button.
You can send the theme, with its summary and top quotes, straight into a Slack channel.
It's a one-off share, not a subscription.
Oh, that's great. That's exactly the Harbor and Pine use case.
And second, we explored a weekly digest email.
Every Monday, you get your top five themes, what's growing, what's new.
We had it going to Slack as well.
I'll be honest, the digest is the thing I'm most excited about.
Half our churn risk is people who just stop logging in.
A digest brings them back without them having to remember.
I like the idea, but I want to flag it's not free.
We don't have any scheduled email infrastructure today.
We'd need notification preferences, unsubscribe handling, deliverability, time zones.
It's a real project, not a feature.
And the Slack version needs the Slack app rebuilt, basically.
The current one can't post rich messages.
Okay. Here's what I'd suggest.
The one-off 'share to Slack' is in scope for the beta, because it's small and it directly addresses the Monday-morning-slides problem.
The weekly digest waits until after the beta, and we use the beta to learn what people would actually want in it.
I can live with that, as long as it doesn't disappear.
It won't. Marcus, can you capture the digest as a follow-on in the roadmap doc, so it doesn't get lost?
Yep. And I'll spec the share to Slack flow for the beta.
What does this look like for a brand new workspace with, like, fifty comments?
Clustering fifty comments is going to give you garbage themes.
Great question, honestly that was the part I was least sure about.
Right now, below a threshold, we show an empty state that says 'themes appear after about two hundred comments,' with a progress bar, and we keep the feed as the fallback view.
Where does the two hundred number come from, by the way?
From the pilot. Below about two hundred comments, most workspaces ended up with a handful of giant themes and a long tail of themes with one or two comments.
Above two hundred, the structure starts to look like something a human would recognize.
And the progress bar makes it feel like a goal instead of an error.
That was the idea, anyway.
I think that's right. I would rather show nothing than show bad themes.
First impressions of the AI are going to stick, especially with the accounts that already distrust the tagging.
Could the empty state import something, though?
Like, connect Zendesk and we backfill the last ninety days?
Then most people would blow past two hundred comments on day one.
Oh, that's a really good idea.
We already have a Zendesk backfill, it's just buried in the settings page.
Surfacing it in onboarding is maybe a day of work.
Okay. I'll put the Zendesk import step right into the onboarding flow.
Before we move on. Are there any objections to Themes being the default view?
This is a big change for existing customers, so I want to make sure we're all okay with it.
Existing customers will definitely be surprised.
Can we give them a toggle for the first month or so?
Some admins have trained their whole team around the feed, and I don't want to generate fifty support tickets on day one.
Related question. What happens to saved filters and scheduled reports that people built on top of the feed?
Some admins have dozens of them.
They keep working, they just live under the feed view.
We're not migrating anything. We did look at converting saved filters into pinned themes, but it's messy, and it's not worth it for the beta.
Good. Honestly the scheduled reports are the thing people would scream about if they broke.
Nothing changes in the reporting pipeline, so they won't break.
I'll double check that the toggle doesn't touch them.
Yes. A 'switch back to feed' toggle, with a note that it goes away later.
I'm totally fine with that.
Okay, so decision: Themes is the default for everyone, with a feed toggle for existing customers during the beta.
Marcus, can you update the prototype with the empty state, the Zendesk import step, and the toggle?
Yep. I'll have the updated prototype ready by end of this week.
Small thing, but can we talk about naming?
'Themes' versus 'Topics'. In the pilot interviews, a couple of people called them topics.
We tested both. Themes won, but only barely.
Six to four, or something like that.
Let's keep Themes for the beta and see what design partners call them without prompting.
That'll tell us more than a vote.
Fair enough.
Okay. Daniel, SSO versus Jira. Walk us through it.
Right. So I wrote a one-pager, I'll drop it in the chat.
The short version is this.
Jira has more requests by count, the eleven accounts, and it's great for retention stories.
SSO has fewer requests, but it's attached to four hundred and twenty thousand in open pipeline.
And it's table stakes for basically every enterprise deal we're going to do next year.
Every security questionnaire asks about it.
Every single one. It's usually question three.
So my recommendation is SAML SSO first, with Okta and Azure AD at launch, plus audit logs, because Globex asked for both.
Then the full Jira integration in Q1.
And in the meantime, we ship the lightweight 'create Jira issue' button from a theme.
One way. Which honestly covers most of what people actually ask for when they say 'Jira integration.'
If we do the button, I want it scoped to exactly that.
No two-way sync, no status updates coming back, nothing.
Otherwise it becomes the full integration by stealth, and then we're back to not having the people.
Agreed. One way, one button.
I'm fine with that. As long as I can tell the eleven accounts it's coming in Q1, with a real date, I can manage the conversation.
And I need a date for SSO that I can put in writing to Globex. What's realistic?
If we start SAML next week with two people, I'd say five weeks to something Globex can actually test, and then a week of hardening.
So roughly six weeks. And I really don't want to promise less than that.
And if it starts slipping, what's the plan?
I don't want Aisha finding out the week it's due.
We'll know by the end of week three.
The spike covers the risky part, and by week three we'll have Okta login working end to end with a real tenant.
If we're behind at that point, I'll tell you and Aisha that day, not at the end.
That's all I need. Victor can handle a heads-up.
He can't handle a surprise.
Six weeks I can sell.
Honestly, I'd much rather give them six and hit it than give them four and slip.
Victor will remember a slip.
Okay, so I'm hearing consensus.
Let me say it back.
We prioritize SAML SSO, with Okta and Azure AD plus audit logs, this quarter, with two engineers, targeting six weeks.
The full Jira integration moves to Q1.
And we ship a one-way 'create Jira issue' button from themes as part of Insights 2.0. Does anyone disagree?
No.
No, sounds good.
Agreed.
Great. That's decided.
Before I write the requirements, let me check a few SAML details with the group, because they affect the estimate.
First, just-in-time provisioning. When someone logs in through Okta for the first time, we create their Driftwood account automatically.
I think that's a must.
Agreed, JIT is a must.
SCIM, for automatic deprovisioning, can come later.
Second, an 'enforce SSO' setting, so admins can require SSO for everyone in the workspace.
And a break-glass admin account that can still log in with a password, in case their identity provider goes down.
Globex asked about exactly that.
Victor wants enforcement, no exceptions except break-glass.
Third, audit logs. My proposed event list is logins, exports, role changes, settings changes, and data deletion.
Retained for one year, viewable in the admin panel.
Globex also asked if they can send audit logs to their SIEM.
They use Splunk, I believe.
Let's do CSV export and an API endpoint for audit logs at launch.
A native Splunk connector can come later.
If they have an API, their security team can pull it into Splunk themselves.
I think Victor will be fine with that. I'll check with him.
One more thing. I'd like Lena to pair on the SAML work.
She did the auth rewrite last year, and she knows where the sharp edges are.
And we should get a security review of the design before we build, not after.
Yes to both. Daniel, can you set up the security review once the requirements doc is drafted?
Will do. I'll schedule a security design review as soon as the draft is ready.
I'll write the SAML requirements doc this week.
It'll cover Okta and Azure AD, the audit log events, and what the admin setup flow looks like.
Raj, can you do a spike on the SAML library so we know whether six weeks is real?
Yes. I'll do the spike and have an estimate I actually trust within three days.
And I'll send Globex and Arcadia our updated security questionnaire answers, with SSO marked as in development.
Daniel, can you review them before I send?
Yep, send them over, I'll turn it around quickly.
I'll let the Jira accounts know it's coming in Q1.
Actually, I'd like to call the two that churned personally.
Maybe we can win one of them back with the button and a date.
Love that. Please do.
Okay, Elena. Launch.
Okay. So, given everything we've just said, here's what I'd propose.
We run a private beta of Insights 2.0 with around twenty design partners, starting in about two weeks.
No big announcement. Just a personal invite from Maya and the account team.
Then general availability once we actually hit the precision bar, and that's when we do the big launch.
Blog post, webinar, customer stories, the whole thing.
For GA I'd like at least three customer stories, ideally one enterprise, one mid-market, and one retail.
And a live webinar where Priya walks through how the themes are built.
People trust AI features more when they see the humans behind them.
Oh no. I mean, yes. Happily.
Priya on a webinar. I love it.
Why twenty design partners?
Enough to generate real merge and split data for Priya.
And small enough that Tom's team can actually talk to every single one of them, every week.
Twenty is about what we can handle.
I'd want a mix. The six pilot accounts who asked for it, plus a few bigger ones, and at least a couple in retail and healthcare, for Priya's data.
And I want to be clear about what a design partner signs up for, so we don't end up with twenty logos who never log in.
My proposal is a thirty minute check-in every week, a shared Slack channel with our team, and a commitment to actually use the themes view for at least four weeks.
And a quote or a case study at GA if it goes well?
Yes, optional, but we ask up front.
People are much more likely to say yes if they know from day one.
I like that. It's a real program, not just early access.
Yes please. Healthcare is our weakest area by far.
Healthcare only after the redaction pass, though.
Right, agreed. Healthcare partners join once redaction is in.
And on messaging. I'd like to test moving away from 'feedback analytics' toward something like 'from feedback to decisions.'
The idea being, we're not another dashboard.
We tell you what to do next.
Can I push back a little?
'From feedback to decisions' is a big promise.
If precision is at seventy-nine during the beta, and a customer makes a decision based on a theme that's actually two themes glued together, that promise hurts us.
That's fair. The way I think about it, the promise is the direction, not a guarantee.
And the merge and split controls are the honest part.
We're saying you stay in control of the themes.
And the dropped summary sentences help.
We're not showing anything we can't support.
Okay. As long as the beta invite doesn't oversell accuracy, I'm fine.
I like that a lot.
It matches the Themes-first design really well.
It'll help in demos for sure.
It's a much simpler story than what we have today.
Let's test it with the beta invite and with the design partners before we commit to it for GA.
Elena, can you draft the messaging brief and the beta invite email?
Yes. I'll have a draft of the messaging brief and the beta invite by early next week.
And Tom, the design partner list?
I'll shortlist twenty design partners, plus a few backups, and share the list at the start of next week.
Can I ask for something for the sales team?
If we're going to talk about Insights 2.0 with prospects during the beta, I need a demo script and a battlecard against the AI insights competitor.
Otherwise everyone will pitch it differently.
Yes. I'd like to do those after we test the messaging with design partners, so we don't train the team on a story we then change.
Say, about two weeks after the invite goes out?
That works. Just not later than that, please. Q4 deals are moving.
Understood. I'll have the demo script and the battlecard ready about two weeks after the beta invite.
And on my side, I'll put together an FAQ for existing customers about the Themes default and the feed toggle, so my team has consistent answers.
We should also do an in-app announcement the first time people see Themes.
I'll add it to the prototype.
Great. Thanks all.
One risk I want to name.
If the precision eval comes back and we're still at seventy-nine, do we still start the beta on schedule?
Good question. My view is yes.
The beta is how we get to eighty-five, through the merge and split data.
But GA is gated on eighty-five.
We don't go GA below that.
That's the right call. I'd be really nervous shipping GA at seventy-nine.
Okay, so that's a decision too.
The beta starts on schedule regardless, and GA is gated on eighty-five percent precision.
What about pricing? Customers are going to ask me what Insights 2.0 costs.
Is it in Pro, is it an add-on?
Honestly, it's not decided. My instinct is that themes are included in Pro, but we put usage caps on the AI summaries, because that's where our costs actually are.
But I need to work the numbers with Helen before I say that to anyone outside this room.
Priya, do you have a rough sense of what the AI actually costs us per workspace?
Roughly. At current volumes, the median workspace costs us about a dollar eighty a month in model costs.
The largest pilot workspace is about fourteen dollars a month.
Almost all of that is the theme summaries, not the clustering itself.
So caps on summaries really are where the leverage is.
Right. Something like, Pro includes summaries for up to fifty thousand comments a month, and above that you move to Business.
That covers almost everyone except the very largest accounts.
From a sales point of view, that's a much easier story than fifteen dollars per seat.
Buyers hate per-seat AI add-ons.
Okay. Good input. But again, none of this leaves the room until Helen and I have run the numbers.
Okay. So for now I tell people pricing will be announced at GA?
Yes. The beta is free for design partners, and pricing comes at GA.
I'll bring a proposal on AI usage caps to the leadership team by end of next week.
Can I see it before leadership?
Packaging affects the launch story.
Of course. I'll share a draft with you and Aisha first.
Okay, we're nearly out of time.
Let me recap owners and dates, and please shout if I get anything wrong.
Priya, the two thousand comment labeled set and the precision report by the middle of next week, plus scoping the redaction pass with Daniel.
Raj, the SAML spike and a real estimate, and the incremental assignment plan with the three second budget.
Daniel, the SAML requirements doc this week.
Marcus, the prototype updates by end of week.
Elena, the messaging brief and beta invite early next week.
Tom, the design partner shortlist at the start of next week, and the Jira churn number.
Aisha, the security questionnaire answers to Globex and Arcadia, once Daniel reviews.
And me, the pricing proposal by end of next week.
And the calls to the two churned accounts.
And those, yes. Did I miss anything?
Can we put a go or no-go on the calendar for the beta?
A few days before it starts, so we can look at the eval results and the latency numbers together, in one room.
Yes, good idea. I'll schedule the beta go or no-go meeting today.
Where does Daniel's one-pager live, by the way?
I want to link it from the eval report.
I'll post it in the Insights project channel right after this, along with the SAML notes.
And I'll post the recording and the notes there too.
For anyone who missed something, the SSO part starts about halfway through.
Could you also drop the timestamps for the decisions in the channel?
Half my team will only watch the SSO part, and that's fine.
Yes, I'll clip the SSO decision and the beta gate so people can watch just those. Two minutes each, tops.
Look at us, finishing on time.
Mark the calendar.
Great meeting. Honestly, this is the first time the launch has felt real to me.
Same. Thanks everyone, this was a really good discussion. Talk soon.
Bye all.
Bye!
